answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of the Lyceum
answer.sourceLine: This is a real Aristotle sentence, and it can be pinned exactly: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 4 (Bekker 1105b), in the English translation W. D. Ross published for Oxford in 1925. The wording is Ross’s — other translators render the same Greek quite differently — but the thought and the sentence structure are Aristotle’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: W. D. Ross, in The Works of Aristotle Translated into English, vol. 9 (Oxford University Press / Humphrey Milford), first edition 1925
4th century BC; dated c. 350 BC by the Internet Classics Archive

source.excerpt: Actions, then, are called just and temperate when they are such as the just or the temperate man would do; but it is not the man who does these that is just and temperate, but the man who also does them as just and temperate men do them. It is well said, then, that it is by doing just acts that the just man is produced, and by doing temperate acts the temperate man; without doing these no one would have even a prospect of becoming good.
trail: The exact wording appears in Book II, chapter 4 of W. D. Ross’s translation, transcribed from The Works of Aristotle Translated into English, vol. 9, at Wikisource ↗, whose header records a first edition of 1925.
A second, independent transcription of the same Ross text carries the identical sentence at the MIT Internet Classics Archive ↗.
Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ lists the line under Nicomachean Ethics Book II with the reference 1105b.9.
Perseus ↗ confirms the passage sits at Bekker page 1105b, section 4, where H. Rackham’s 1934 Loeb translation gives the same argument in different English.
source.excerptNote: W. D. Ross’s translation, Nicomachean Ethics II.4. The sentence immediately after this one is Aristotle’s complaint that most people “take refuge in theory” instead.

sourceLink.text: Read Book II in Ross’s translation at Wikisource

source.rightsNote: Aristotle’s Greek has been out of copyright for centuries, and the English shown here is W. D. Ross’s translation, first published in 1925 by Oxford University Press / Humphrey Milford — before the 1931 US threshold, so it is public domain in the United States. Note that this applies to Ross’s wording specifically: later renderings, such as H. Rackham’s 1934 Loeb version, are separate works with their own status.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Aristotle
author.bio: Aristotle studied for twenty years under Plato, tutored the young Alexander of Macedon, and founded his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens. The Nicomachean Ethics — probably lecture material rather than a polished book, and named for his son Nicomachus — is where he argues that character is not something you are born with or reason your way into, but something you build by repetition. Virtue, on his account, is a skill: you become just the way you become a builder or a harpist, by doing the thing badly until you do it well.

misattribution.heading: The line people quote instead
misattribution.intro: This sentence is authentic, so the problem here is not a fake — it is a substitution. The version of this idea that actually circulates under Aristotle’s name was written in the twentieth century by an American popular historian, and the English of the real sentence belongs to a translator who is almost never named.

items.scope: "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit."
items.why: Durant wrote this while summarising Aristotle’s ethics in The Story of Philosophy (1926), p. 87: “Excellence is an art won by training and habituation … we are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act but a habit.” His own footnote points the reader to Nicomachean Ethics ii, 4 — the very chapter this page’s sentence comes from (Quote/Unquote ↗, Wikiquote ↗).

Aristotle wrote in Greek; “It is well said, then …” is Ross’s 1925 phrasing (Wikisource ↗). H. Rackham’s 1934 Loeb renders the same Greek as “a man becomes just by doing just actions and temperate by doing temperate actions” (Perseus ↗) — so quoting these words as Aristotle’s exact words is a half-truth worth naming.

misattribution.truthLine: Aristotle did write this, in Greek, in Nicomachean Ethics Book II, chapter 4 — cited as 1105b.9 in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗. What he did not write is the tidier “excellence is a habit” slogan that took its place.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Aristotle is answering an objection he raises against himself. If you only become just by doing just things, but a just act is by definition what a just person does, the whole thing looks circular — you would need the virtue before you could ever acquire it. His way out is that the beginner’s just act and the just person’s just act are not the same act. The beginner does the right thing clumsily, for mixed reasons, without settled character; the just person does it knowingly, chooses it for its own sake, and does it from a stable disposition.

That is why the sentence lands where it does in the chapter. Doing the acts is not sufficient for virtue — but it is absolutely necessary, and Aristotle’s next line is a jab at people who skip it: most of them “take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way.”
detailsBody: The Greek verb behind Ross’s “is produced” carries the sense of coming to be — character as something that emerges over time rather than something switched on. Aristotle’s working analogy earlier in Book II is craft: people become builders by building and harpists by playing the harp, and they become just, temperate and brave the same way.

Two thousand years later Will Durant compressed this whole chapter into a single memorable line for a popular audience — and that compression, not Aristotle’s own sentence, is what most people now quote as “Aristotle.”
context.pull: You do not reason your way into good character. You practise your way into it.
